To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the inflected curve can be predicted without appeal to any heterogeneity of the cell population, and that (b) the inflected survival curve is not necessarily indicative of the presence of a heterogeneous cell population.

(i) the inflected survival curve is a consequence of the distribution of cells through the replication cycle; (ii) this distribution is itself a consequence of the exponential nature of cell division; (iii) the exponential nature of the distribution is a consequence of exponential growth of the culture.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mathematical description of the process of killing of bacterial cells by ultraviolet irradiation.
the construction of a mathematical model of the survival curves of bacteria exposed to ultraviolet light, and with a comparison of the predictions of the model with experimental data.
the mathematical analysis of the effects of ionizing and non-ionizing radiation on biological systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two mechanisms mentioned above, when combined with the replication cycle, are sufficient to explain all observed types of radiation survival curve for bacteria, including the inflected curve.

the observed survival curves for ultraviolet irradiation of bacteria are all consistent with the hypothesis that killing occurs when a portion of the DNA is excised from the intact molecule, and that the observed variety of shapes of the curves is due entirely to the distribution of cells in the various stages of the replication cycle.
the inflected curve is not a “multi-hit” curve.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for the case of bacteria, the observed types of survival curves can be explained in terms of a simple mathematical model, which does not invoke the existence of subpopulations with different radiation sensitivities, and which does not require the existence of any special mechanism for repair of radiation damage.
, in the absence of any other information, one may expect the inflection to occur at a dose of about 1.4 times the dose required for a single-hit kill.

the observed survival curves are consistent with the hypothesis that lethality occurs when a damaged DNA strand is not repaired, and that the various shapes observed are due to a variety of factors, including the distribution through the cell cycle of cells in exponential growth, the distribution of the repair mechanism, and the distribution of the damage in the population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the inflected curve is a consequence of the distribution of cells through the replication cycle, and not a result of heterogeneity of the cell population.
, if one considers only two mechanisms, namely the excision repair and the replication fork interference, one can explain all the observed types of survival curves.
, for any particular survival curve, there is a model of DNA repair and damage that is consistent with the data.
